The post Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Nace AI has released Drex for Search , which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question. TL;DR Size: a hosted search system built to search over 1M+ files. It pairs with an answering model such as GPT-5, Gemini 3.5 Flash or Qwen 27B. Runs on: Nace’s managed cloud, a dedicated cloud, your own AWS or Azure account, or on-prem and air-gapped. Performance: ranked #1 or #2 on 3 of 4 public leaderboards, per Nace. Best: 77.5% R@1 on VisDocAgentBench, 10 points above Claude Opus 5 (67.5%). What did Nace AI release? Nace AI frames search as a series of decisions. Drex for Search applies its Drex models to those decisions. Drex scores given options with a calibrated probability each, in 1 forward pass. That makes it cheap enough for every agent step. The release targets classic RAG, which Nace sums up as chunk, embed, top-k, hope. The pipeline breaks in 3 cases: the answer sits in a table on page 23 the answer needs 2 hops across files the answer is inside a scanned PDF How does Drex for Search work inside an agent? Nace describes 3 steps: Classify: Before any search runs, Drex decides if the question needs a quick lookup or an agent. The agent route reads documents and queries tables. Squeeze: Drex walks the workspace level by level: folder, file, section, page. Inside a sheet, it narrows to table and column. Each level keeps only what can hold the answer. Answer: Only the kept pages and tables reach the LLM. The answer cites the file and page. Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand. How much does it help coding agents? Nace AI tested 9 agent and model pairs on OfficeQA Pro , a 133-question benchmark over U.S. Treasury Bulletins. Key highlights: 6% more answers right, 62% fewer steps, 56% fewer tokens, and 2.3x faster. The post vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. TL;DR Size: 26.09B parameters (dense, including a 0.46B vision encoder); 131,072 tokens of context per question. Runs on: tested on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with BF16 weights; no official quantized variant is listed yet. Performance: highest SR-Text score of the 6 decision models in the team’s own private test. Best: 97.8 on SR-Text tools and automation (chance-corrected accuracy). Worst: 54.6% on SR-Box (9 domains), 5.0 points below its sibling d3-turbo. What is d3-ultra? d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Choice: pick 1 of several options. Yes / No: return the probability of yes. Score: rate on a scale. Box: locate something in an image or a video moment. Track: follow a target across a whole video. Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. How does d3-ultra work? The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. How does d3-ultra perform on benchmarks? The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra: 87.2 GLiDE V1.2: 85.1 d1-ultra: 83.4 d3-turbo: 83.1 d3: 81.4 Jev 1.14: 73.1 d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. How do you deploy d3-ultra? There are 4 routes: Transformers: AutoModel.from_pretrained("vllm-sr/d3-ultra", trust_remote_code=True) with transformers==5.17.0 . The optional flash-linear-attention package adds fast GPU kernels. vLLM Semantic Router Engine: vllm-sr serve -e vllm-sr/d3-ultra , added in PR #5449 on October 25, 2026. Free API: the card says decision.vllm-sr.ai serves d3-ultra, with a free key. Demo: the official Hugging Face Space . d3-ultra vs GLiDE V1.2, d1-ultra, Jev 1.14 and d3-turbo Feature d3-ultra d3-turbo GLiDE V1.2 d1-ultra Jev 1.14 Developer vLLM Semantic Router vLLM Semantic Router Fastino Labs Liquid AI TypeSafe Parameters 26.09B 26.09B 26B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context per question 131,072 32,768 default; 131,072 with long_context 40,000 default 32,768 262,144 Weights / license Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Fastino Community License Hosted only Hosted only, proprietary Inputs Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images Text, images Text, images Box / track Box + track Box + track No No Box only SR-Text (self-reported by vLLM-SR) 87.2 83.1 85.1 83.4 73.1 SR-Box, 10 domains 58.2% 60.0% Not supported Not supported 45.7% Public index score Submitted, not yet on board 70.2 Jev DI (own estimate) 71.5 Decision Index 0.4.1 65 AA Decision Index 57 AA Decision Index Price Free API, self-host Free API, self-host $0.04 / M input $0.042 / M input $0.042 / M input Key Takeaways d3-ultra is a 27B Apache-2.0 decision model that never generates text. It reads input once: 255 questions about 1 photo take 2.16 s. It tops the team’s SR-Text test at 87.2, ahead of GLiDE V1.2 at 85.1. It trails d3-turbo on Box grounding: 58.2% vs 60.0%. It reads text, images and video once, then returns probabilities for every answer, scoring 87.2 on the team’s SR-Text test. The post vLLM Semantic Router Releases d3-ultra: A 27B Open Multimodal Decision Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The vLLM Semantic Router team has released d3-ultra , a 27B multimodal decision model under Apache-2.0. The d3-ultra decision model does not generate text. It reads an input once and returns a probability for every answer to every question. For developers, that means routing, classification, visual grounding and video checks from 1 open-weight call. TL;DR Size: 26.09B parameters (dense, including a 0.46B vision encoder); 131,072 tokens of context per question. Runs on: tested on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with BF16 weights; no official quantized variant is listed yet. Performance: highest SR-Text score of the 6 decision models in the team’s own private test. Best: 97.8 on SR-Text tools and automation (chance-corrected accuracy). Worst: 54.6% on SR-Box (9 domains), 5.0 points below its sibling d3-turbo. What is d3-ultra? d3-ultra is a System One decision model from vLLM Semantic Router that answers typed questions with probabilities. It is the newest member of Decision 3.0 , a family that spans 0.6B to 27B. You send a state (text or JSON, plus images or videos) and a set of questions. Each question has a type: Choice: pick 1 of several options. Yes / No: return the probability of yes. Score: rate on a scale. Box: locate something in an image or a video moment. Track: follow a target across a whole video. Images can also sit inside questions and options. A quiz can show a photo, then offer 4 etchings as answers. How does d3-ultra work? The core idea is state once . The model reads the input once per request and answers every question from that single read. The config shows a Qwen3.5-architecture backbone with 64 layers. 48 are linear-attention layers and 16 are full-attention layers. The card does not name its base checkpoint. vLLM’s recipe says the sibling d3 was trained from Qwen3.8-27B. Box answers always return exactly 1 box with a confidence. A confidence near 0 means the target is not in the picture. Questions over 131,072 tokens fail with max_length_exceeded ; nothing is silently truncated. How does d3-ultra perform on benchmarks? The research team compares d3-ultra with GLiDE V1.2 , d1-ultra, d3-turbo, d3 and Jev 1.14 on 2 in-house tests. SR-Text has 10,411 text requests with 73,495 questions. Most recreate skills from 34 public benchmarks with new items. Another 4,896 questions come from 43 new task families, like SQL checks and ticket routing. Scores are chance-corrected: 0 is chance, 100 is perfect. d3-ultra: 87.2 GLiDE V1.2: 85.1 d1-ultra: 83.4 d3-turbo: 83.1 d3: 81.4 Jev 1.14: 73.1 d3-ultra leads every area except arts and human taste. There, d1-ultra scores 90.8 against 89.6, within the margin of error. SR-Box has 5,678 Box questions on 4,984 images across 10 domains. A box counts as correct at IoU 0.5 or higher. d3-ultra scores 58.2% over 10 domains and 54.6% over 9. d3-turbo scores 60.0% and 59.6%. Jev 1.14 scores 45.7% and 46.9%. The team says d3-turbo stays stronger on natural images, while d3-ultra leads on charts. Latency: on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X with AutoModel, 1 question about a photo takes 304 ms. 255 questions take 2.16 s, about 7.3 ms per extra question. How do you deploy d3-ultra? There are 4 routes: Transformers: AutoModel.from_pretrained("vllm-sr/d3-ultra", trust_remote_code=True) with transformers==5.17.0 . The optional flash-linear-attention package adds fast GPU kernels. vLLM Semantic Router Engine: vllm-sr serve -e vllm-sr/d3-ultra , added in PR #5449 on October 25, 2026. Free API: the card says decision.vllm-sr.ai serves d3-ultra, with a free key. Demo: the official Hugging Face Space . d3-ultra vs GLiDE V1.2, d1-ultra, Jev 1.14 and d3-turbo Feature d3-ultra d3-turbo GLiDE V1.2 d1-ultra Jev 1.14 Developer vLLM Semantic Router vLLM Semantic Router Fastino Labs Liquid AI TypeSafe Parameters 26.09B 26.09B 26B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context per question 131,072 32,768 default; 131,072 with long_context 40,000 default 32,768 262,144 Weights / license Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Apache-2.0 Open, Fastino Community License Hosted only Hosted only, proprietary Inputs Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images, video Text, JSON, images Text, images Text, images Box / track Box + track Box + track No No Box only SR-Text (self-reported by vLLM-SR) 87.2 83.1 85.1 83.4 73.1 SR-Box, 10 domains 58.2% 60.0% Not supported Not supported 45.7% Public index score Submitted, not yet on board 70.2 Jev DI (own estimate) 71.5 Decision Index 0.4.1 65 AA Decision Index 57 AA Decision Index Price Free API, self-host Free API, self-host $0.04 / M input $0.042 / M input $0.042 / M input Key Takeaways d3-ultra is a 27B Apache-2.0 decision model that never generates text. It reads input once: 255 questions about 1 photo take 2.16 s. It tops the team’s SR-Text test at 87.2, ahead of GLiDE V1.2 at 85.1. It trails d3-turbo on Box grounding: 58.2% vs 60.0%. All benchmark numbers are self-reported on private test sets. Check out the model card , the GitHub repo , the Decision 3.0 collection and the Hugging Face Space . The 3B model parses books, filings and reports of hundreds of pages in one request. Its core change is SR-SWA, a sparse attention scheme that keeps per-step decoding cost nearly flat. Weights ship under the MIT license , with code on GitHub . TL;DR Size: 3.34B parameters . Active parameters not disclosed. Max position length 131,072 tokens. Runs on: 1 CUDA GPU in BF16. Baidu tested on an NVIDIA A800-80GB. BF16 weights total about 6.7 GB. Performance: first place on both multi-page benchmarks Baidu tested, against 9 other models (self-reported). Best: 77.1 overall on MarathonDocBench (hundreds of pages). The next model, Kimi-K3, scores 33.7. Worst: 48.2 on heading hierarchy (TEDS) on MarathonDocBench, its lowest sub-score. The post Mirendil Launches Fern 0.1, Its First Model, With 10M-Token Context appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Mirendil has released Fern , its first AI model. Mirendil Fern is a from-scratch coding model with a context window of up to 10M tokens. Mirendil explains how that equals about 23 MB of code, or roughly half a million lines. That is a codebase on the scale of Megatron-LM, held in context at once. Fern 0.1 is the first version, built from Mirendil-Base after a short round of post-training. For developers, its like, you load a whole repo, a full training log or days of agent traces at once. TL;DR Size: 0.1 to 0.5T parameters (exact count and active params not disclosed); context up to 10M tokens. Runs on: Hosted early access only; no open weights or quantized builds announced. Performance: Strong long-context retrieval, mid-pack agentic coding versus open-weight models, well behind frontier models. Best: 100% on RULER single-needle retrieval at every length from 32K to 10M tokens (base model). Worst: 6.1% on Terminal Bench 4.0, versus 66.4% for Claude Opus 5.5 in Mirendil’s own table. What is Mirendil Fern? Fern is a language model from Mirendil , an AI R&D lab. Fern is aimed at AI R&D work, not general chat. Mirendil lists 6 target uses: Working across larger codebases Agentic coding that runs commands until tests pass Research code: training loops, data pipelines and evaluations Debugging training runs from long logs and stack traces Reading full agent or training traces end to end Auditing pretraining shards for duplicates, contamination and junk How was Fern built? Fern sits on Mirendil-Base , which Mirendil says one researcher pretrained in 3.5 months. Total compute was under $10M, including experiments, agent token spend and data processing. AI agents wrote over 99% of the code. The researcher chose what to try and when to intervene. Training data came only from public sources: GitHub, public code, web pages and public datasets. Mirendil says it used no distillation, no synthetic data and no licensed data. The code was written from scratch on PyTorch and JAX. Fern is the smallest of 3 planned models. Mirendil-Base-Large (0.5 to 2T parameters) is over 80% through pretraining. Mirendil-Base-XL (2 to 10T) is over 20% through. Does longer context actually help? Mirendil tested next-token prediction on its own repositories, concatenated into a 42.9 MB stream. It measured cross-entropy in bits per byte, where lower is better. Window sizes here are measured in bytes, not tokens. Fern’s loss fell from 0.246 at a 32K-byte window to 0.155 at 16M and 23M bytes. The other models were scored up to about 1M tokens, their advertised limit. At a 1M-byte window, Kimi-K3 scored 0.140 and Fern 0.165. So Fern is not the best predictor at equal context. Its advantage is that the curve keeps going past where others stop. How does Fern score on RULER? RULER is a standard long-context benchmark. Mirendil ran 5 RULER tasks on Mirendil-Base, the pre-post-training model. It used greedy decoding, thinking off and exact string matching. Multi-hop reasoning drops to 45% at 10M. Each 10M cell uses only 20 examples, versus 100 elsewhere. Mirendil says broader long-context results are coming. How does Fern 0.1 do on agentic benchmarks? This kind of egalitarianism seems unusual given that startup prospectuses usually show a founding CEO with a much larger relative stake compared to co-founders. The company’s co-founders include Dario Amodei , Daniela Amodei , Tom Brown , Jack Clark , Jared Kaplan , Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah . Anthropic’s risk factors take up 93 pages of its IPO filing So, is investing in Anthropic a risky bet? Anthropic certainly seems to think so. The company’s IPO prospectus contains a staggering 93 pages of risk factors. They start at page 27 and end on page 120. Some are pretty mundane. For instance, the company is concerned that slower revenue growth could potentially constrain its ability to fund frontier AI development and attract and retain top talent. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:13:12 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Crunchbase Data Shows Q3 Robotics Startup Funding Jumps 185% As US And China Lead Physical AI Push https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-us-china-robotics-startup-funding-jumps-physical-ai-push/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 11:00:53 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94284 Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with the bulk of investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it. I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered , we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to. Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered. Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years. Gartner , meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review. Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling. Start with work that already has a rulebook The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement. Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified. Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls. McKinsey ‘s most recent State of AI research found that the small group of companies seeing significant bottom-line returns from AI, about 6% of respondents, were nearly 3x as likely to have fundamentally redesigned their workflows. In my experience, that redesign starts with writing the rule down. If a new hire couldn’t follow your description of a decision on the person’s first day, an agent won’t follow it either. Set autonomy by workflow Tech execs I speak with often ask whether an AI system is autonomous, as if that were a fixed property of the product. In practice, the same agent should run with different levels of freedom depending on what it touches. At Get Covered, we configure each agent on different levels. For instance, a reminder to a vendor whose certificate expires next month can go out automatically. A response to a resident who has requested an emotional support animal never does. Today, we help 25,000 Shopify brands simplify gnarly workflows like inventory, bundling, and order fulfillment (for even the world's largest brands like Sennheiser, Godiva, YAMAHA, and Stanley Drinkware). Tomorrow, we'll deliver intelligent automation that feels like an on-site operations team so merchants can focus on building their brand.</p> <p>We're a fully-remote and bootstrapped company with teammates around the world. We love what we do and love who we build for. We're a small team of 9 (3 Support specialists) who amplify each other's work by working closely together: dev with support, support with marketing, and so on. We're curious, kind, scrappy yet rigorous, and highly intentional. If this sounds like the type of team you'd like to be a part of, we'd love to hear from you.</p> <h2>About this role</h2> <p>In this role, you'll have significant ownership of your work, make impactful decisions daily, and report directly to the founders. This is a full-time remote position open to candidates in all timezones.</p> <p>Support is the foundation of everything we do. Our apps have consistently maintained high ratings on the Shopify App Store because our support team genuinely cares about helping merchants succeed. As one of our early support hires, you'll get to know our products inside and out and become a go-to expert on how things work under the hood.</p> <p>We hire slowly and keep the bar high, so the people you work with every day will be some of the best you’ve worked with. You'll be joining a small but growing support team, where we all wear many hats. You'll need strong troubleshooting instincts, a curious mind, and a willingness to get into the weeds. You should feel comfortable making judgment calls on UX or product questions, and know when something needs to be escalated. There's plenty of room to grow with us.</p> <h2>What we're looking for</h2> <ul> <li>Somone who fixes the process while you’re fixing the ticket.</li> <li>Someone who's comfortable diving into technical issues and can confidently support merchants over email and through clear, helpful video recordings.</li> <li>A strong track record in customer-facing roles, with a focus on delivering thoughtful, efficient support. You listen closely, ask the right questions, and know how to turn a frustrating situation into a positive experience.</li> <li>Good judgment around what needs to be escalated and what doesn't. You'll know when to loop in teammates and how to make that handoff seamless for the merchant.</li> <li>An eye for patterns and the ability to turn merchant feedback into actionable insights for our product and engineering teams.</li> <li>The ability to prioritize effectively. You can assess what's urgent, what's important, and what can wait, especially when everything feels like it needs attention.</li> <li>Comfort with change. You stay calm when the product evolves and enjoy picking up new knowledge as you go.</li> <li>A team-first mindset. You jump in to support others, document what you've learned, and share what's working so we can all move faster together.</li> <li>Strong communication skills, especially in writing. You know how to keep things clear, friendly, and easy to follow, whether you're talking to a merchant or a teammate.</li> <li>Natural troubleshooting instincts. You enjoy working on tricky issues and figuring out what's actually going on, not just treating the symptoms.</li> <li>Great attention to detail. You care about getting the small things right, because they add up to a better experience.</li> <li>A curious mind. You're always learning, always testing, always a few steps ahead.</li> <li>The ability to explain complex ideas in a simple way, especially for merchants who aren't technical.</li> </ul> <h2>Experience</h2> <ul> <li>Previous experience in technical support at a SaaS or tech company</li> <li>Familiarity with HelpScout or other ticketing systems</li> <li>Hands-on knowledge of front-end development (HTML, CSS, browser dev tools)</li> <li>Working understanding of REST APIs and common data formats like JSON or XML</li> <li>Comfort with debugging using Chrome DevTools, especially for browser or front-end issues</li> <li>Knowledge of how HTTP and DNS work</li> <li>Experience reading API documentation and troubleshooting third-party integrations or custom app setups</li> <li>Some exposure to GraphQL APIs</li> </ul> <h2>Bonus experience</h2> <ul> <li>Shopify theme development and Liquid: Knowing how themes interact with app blocks, line item properties, and cart/checkout logic helps when diagnosing visual or UX issues on merchant stores.</li> <li>Understanding of Shopify's admin and storefront APIs: Familiarity with how Shopify's APIs behave (especially in headless or custom setups) can be useful when troubleshooting sync issues, metafields, or app-triggered updates.</li> </ul> <h2>Beyond expertise, success in this role means embodying 3 core values</h2> <ol> <li><strong>Resourcefulness:</strong> You're relentlessly resourceful and always find ways to achieve the highest standards of quality. You know where to look and whom to consult when faced with challenges.</li> <li><strong>Ownership:</strong> You take complete ownership and pride in your work. This means deeply understanding our existing and prospective merchants, as well as our product.</li> <li><strong>Communication:</strong> You're clear, thoughtful, and intentional in how you communicate with both merchants and teammates. You surface issues early, share relevant context, and keep things moving without needing constant follow-up.</li> </ol> <h2>We're async by default</h2> <p>If you've ever ended a day of back-to-back meetings wondering when you were supposed to get any actual work done, we get it. We've been there. We've built a culture that protects time, encourages focus, and trusts you to do great work without constant check-ins.</p> <p>We meet once a week for 30 min on Mondays. The rest of the time, we default to async: clear Slack threads, thoughtful Looms, and shared docs.</p> <h2>Perks &amp; compensation</h2> <ul> <li>Competitive salary + annual pay increases.</li> <li>$1,000 annual workspace stipend for laptop, headphones, or that standing desk you've been eyeing.</li> <li>Flexible hours. It matches HNSW accuracy at 90% recall using 4 GB instead of 188 GB, at the cost of seconds-level search. The post Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab built LEANN , an open-source vector index that stores almost no embeddings. The LEANN vector index recomputes embeddings at query time instead of saving them to disk. The repo benchmark shows a 60 million chunk Wikipedia index dropping from 201 GB to 6 GB. The research paper won the Best Research Paper award at MLSys 2026 . So, it brings semantic search and RAG over personal data, on a laptop. TL;DR Size: 6 GB for 60M chunks ( repo ); 4 GB in the paper’s 76 GB Wikipedia setup. Default embedder: Contriever (110M params). It is an index, not an LLM, so no context length applies. Runs on: laptops and workstations. The paper tested an RTX 4090 box with 32 GB RAM and an M1 Ultra Mac. A CPU-only Linux install exists, with no published CPU latency. Performance: matches HNSW downstream accuracy at 90% recall, using under 5% of raw-data storage. Best: 25.5% NQ accuracy, identical to HNSW, using 4 GB instead of 188 GB. Worst: HotpotQA retrieval takes 44.80 s on the Mac, 50.1% of total pipeline time. What is LEANN? LEANN is a low-storage approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index built on top of FAISS . It targets one problem: vector indexes are often bigger than the data they index. The research paper shows a 76 GB corpus needs 173 GB of embeddings plus a 15 GB HNSW graph. That more than doubles the raw data. LEANN keeps a pruned graph, drops the full vectors, and rebuilds them on demand. The code is MIT licensed and installs with uv pip install leann . How does LEANN recompute embeddings without stalling search? Graph indexes like HNSW visit only a small set of nodes per query. LEANN exploits that. It stores the graph plus a compact product quantization (PQ) table. At query time, it re-embeds only nodes on the search path. 3 techniques keep this practical: Two-level search: cheap PQ distances rank neighbors first. Only top candidates get exact recomputation. Dynamic batching: candidates from several hops are grouped, for example 64 at once, for GPU efficiency. High-degree preserving pruning: most nodes keep few edges, while the top 2% “hub” nodes keep more. In ablations, two-level search gives an average 1.4x speedup. Adding batching raises it to 1.8x. Embedding recomputation still accounts for about 76% of query latency. How does LEANN perform on benchmarks? The research team tested NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA and HotpotQA against a 60M-passage RPJ-Wiki datastore. Latency is measured at 90% Recall@3. All figures below are self-reported in the research paper . On NQ, with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN and HNSW both reach 25.5% downstream accuracy. LEANN uses 4 GB of storage. HNSW uses 188 GB. BM25 scores 18.3%, and PQ compression scores 17.9%. The cost is search time. LEANN retrieval takes 2.48 s on NQ, versus 0.05 s for HNSW. Generation takes about 20 s, so end-to-end latency rises from 20.95 s to 23.34 s. Across datasets on the RTX 4090, LEANN retrieval ranges from 1.12 s (GPQA) to 7.12 s (HotpotQA). The IVF-based recomputation baseline, inspired by EdgeRAG , is up to 200x slower. LEANN improves exact match by up to 11.8% over BM25. The GitHub repo reports similar savings on personal data. 400K chat messages shrink from 1.8 GB to 64 MB. 38K browser entries shrink from 130 MB to 6.4 MB. LEANN vs other vector indexes Feature LEANN HNSW (FAISS) DiskANN IVF-Recompute (EdgeRAG-style) PQ compression Approach Pruned graph, recompute on demand Graph plus all vectors in RAM Graph and vectors on SSD, PQ in RAM IVF clusters, recompute on demand Compressed vectors plus graph Storage, 76 GB corpus 4 GB 188 GB 270 GB Below 5% of raw data 20 GB NQ retrieval at 90% recall (RTX 4090) 2.48 s 0.05 s 0.03 s 307.61 s Fails to reach 90% HotpotQA retrieval at 90% recall (RTX 4090) 7.12 s 0.05 s 0.11 s 429.46 s Fails to reach 90% NQ downstream accuracy (Qwen3-4B) 25.5% 25.5% Not disclosed Not disclosed 17.9% Fits 32 GB RAM workstation Yes No (OOM) Yes Yes Yes License MIT MIT MIT Not disclosed Varies by implementation Storage, latency and accuracy figures come from the LEANN paper v2 , Tables 1 and 2 and Section 7.2 (self-reported). License and design rows link to each project’s own source. Where can developers use LEANN? The repo ships ready apps for documents, Apple Mail, Chrome history, WeChat, iMessage, and ChatGPT or Claude exports. MCP readers pull live data from Slack and Twitter bookmarks. LEANN also runs as a semantic search MCP server for Claude Code . On 30 SWE-Bench Pro tasks from ContextBench, the team reports 24.2% initial relevant-code recall versus 11.4% for BM25. The agent also used 8.4% fewer tokens. HNSW is the default backend, with DiskANN for faster search. Generation works with Ollama, Hugging Face, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible API. It supports Ubuntu, Arch, WSL, macOS and Windows. Some apps, like Apple Mail search, are macOS only. Key Takeaways LEANN stores a pruned graph and recomputes embeddings at query time. 60M chunks: 201 GB down to 6 GB in the repo benchmark. Matches HNSW accuracy (25.5% on NQ) at 90% recall. Search costs seconds: 2.48 s vs 0.05 s for HNSW on NQ. MIT licensed and an MLSys 2026 Best Research Paper. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and PyPI package .
